What Is Fun With Feet?

Fun With Feet is an online marketplace, launched around 2021, built specifically for buying and selling photos and videos of feet.

It's operated by GYCO Online Limited, a company registered in England and Wales, with an address at Kemp House, City Road, London.

That UK registration matters in a niche where a lot of platforms are anonymous or offshore, and it's a genuine point in the platform's favour.

The model is simple. Creators sign up, verify their identity, build a profile, upload feet content, and set their own prices.

Buyers browse profiles, view free previews, and pay to unlock full galleries or individual items. Sellers can also accept direct messages for custom requests, which typically earn more than off-the-shelf content.

The platform markets itself as “the most fun and trusted platform,” advertises that it's “trusted by 8,000+ buyers,” and keeps content strictly feet-focused, with no general nudity.

A few things stand out immediately. Every creator is ID-verified, which the platform describes as a manual review for quality and authenticity.

Browsing and purchases are designed to be anonymous and discreet. And the whole experience is niche by design: buyers who are there want feet, not unrelated content.

If you're wondering about a “Fun With Feet app,” there isn't a dedicated one. Everything runs through the website in a browser — which becomes relevant later, because several reviewers describe the mobile web experience as glitchy. If a dedicated sell feet pics app matters to you, that's worth weighing early.

How Does Fun With Feet Work?

From a seller's point of view, getting started takes about an hour, and the flow is genuinely beginner-friendly. You create an account, confirm you're 18 or older, and accept the terms.

You choose a subscription plan, because unlike buying, selling isn't free. You then verify your identity with a government-issued ID, which the platform is legally required to check.

After verification, you add a payment method for the subscription, set up your bank details for withdrawals, and build your profile with a bio and picture.

From there you upload content, organise it into galleries, and set your prices. New sellers commonly price single photos between $5 and $15, with videos and custom work higher.

When a buyer purchases, the money lands in your Fun With Feet balance, and you request a withdrawal to your bank.

That last step — the withdrawal — is where the most serious complaints appear, and we'll come back to it in detail.

Here's the part the marketing skips: nothing in this flow brings you buyers. You have a shop, but the platform doesn't send shoppers to it.

That's the difference between a storefront and a marketplace, and it quietly determines whether you make money.

Fun With Feet Pricing and Fees: What You Actually Pay

Fun With Feet charges creators a subscription rather than a per-sale commission.

The most commonly cited pricing is around $9.99 for three months or $14.99 for six months, and some sellers have reported changes to those figures over time.

Buyers pay nothing to join; they only pay for the content they choose to unlock at your prices.

On fees, the platform's own seller FAQ is clear: Fun With Feet does not take a commission from seller earnings, and creators keep 100% of what they make.

That's a real advantage on paper compared with platforms that take a percentage of every sale.

Treat any third-party claim of a fixed commission with caution, because it conflicts with the platform's stated position. The honest summary: the meaningful cost is the upfront subscription, not a cut of your sales.

And that upfront subscription is the catch. You pay it before you've made a single sale — and, as we cover below, the refund policy specifically doesn't cover you if the sales never come.

For a beginner with no outside audience, that's money spent on access to a shop with very little foot traffic.

Reader-first takeaway: The commission model is generous, but commission only matters once you're making sales. The real question is whether the platform helps you get those first sales — and its low, no-commission pricing is only a genuine advantage if you can bring your own buyers.

The Core Issue: Storefront vs Marketplace

This is the single most important thing to understand before you choose a platform, and almost no review explains it clearly.

A marketplace actively surfaces sellers to buyers. It has search, categories, rankings, and algorithmic discovery, so a brand-new creator can get views and sales without an existing audience.

FeetFinder works this way, which is why new sellers there report a genuine path to their first sales.

A storefront is just a page that lives on a website. It looks professional, handles payments, and keeps you anonymous — but it doesn't send you shoppers. If nobody knows your page exists, nobody visits it.

Fun With Feet operates much closer to a storefront: you're given the shop, and you're expected to be the marketer who fills it with buyers, usually by promoting on Reddit, Instagram, TikTok, or X.

This isn't a criticism of the platform's honesty; it's a description of its architecture. And it explains the most common Fun With Feet experience almost perfectly.

A seller uploads in week one, checks a flat dashboard for weeks, and only sees activity once they start driving their own traffic from elsewhere.

Sellers often read that silence as “the platform is dead” or “this is a scam,” when it's really a mismatch between what they expected and how the platform is built.

If you already have an audience, a storefront is fine — even efficient. If you don't, a storefront is the hardest possible way to start, and a marketplace is what you actually need.

Is Fun With Feet Legit, or a Scam?

Let's answer the exact question people search. No, Fun With Feet is not a scam in the legal sense.

It's a real, operating company registered in England and Wales, it processes genuine payments, it verifies identities, and many sellers do get paid. If you're worried the site itself is out to defraud you, that framing isn't supported by the evidence.

However, “legitimate” and “worth your money” are two very different things.

A meaningful number of sellers describe an experience that feels, in their words, like a scam, for two reasons.

First, they pay the subscription and make no sales, then discover the refund policy doesn't cover that situation.

Second, and more seriously, several reviewers report requesting a payout of money they'd already earned and not receiving it — sometimes for weeks, with support going quiet.

On Trustpilot, one seller writing on 30 May 2026 said they requested a payout that, more than a month later, was still marked as “Request,” that they'd given support two seven-day deadlines which were both ignored, and that their account was active and verified the whole time.

Another reviewer reported not receiving a withdrawal after meeting the minimum, and said support ignored their payout emails but processed their subscription cancellation.

These are individual accounts, not a court finding — but they're specific, dated, and consistent enough to take seriously.

So the accurate verdict: Fun With Feet is a legitimate platform, not a fraud, but it carries a real, documented risk of frustration around getting paid, and that risk deserves to weigh on your decision.

Fun With Feet Trustpilot and Reddit Reviews: What Sellers Really Say

On the surface, Fun With Feet's Trustpilot looks strong: roughly 4.5 out of 5 from about 77 reviews at the time of writing.

Look closer, though, and a pattern emerges that changes how you should read that score.

First, the profile is a claimed, paid Trustpilot profile, the company is categorised there as a marketing agency, and it actively invites customers to leave reviews.

A large share of the five-star reviews are from invited users and are about the sign-up experience — lines like “easy to set up,” “super easy to sign up,” and “quick and easy.”

Those are real, but they're reviews of registration, not of earning money, and many are written days after joining, before any sales could realistically happen.

The critical reviews tell a different, more detailed story, and they're almost all about what happens after you actually try to use the platform.

One reviewer wrote that after less than a week on FeetFinder they had more profile views than in a whole month on Fun With Feet, called the upload experience “awful” and unusable on mobile, described “zero traffic,” and ended with “my advice, go to Feet Finder.”

Another, giving three stars, said it's “very difficult to get sales, especially if you want to be more discreet.” Others reported the site crashing repeatedly and payouts going unpaid. Trustpilot itself notes the company hasn't replied to its negative reviews.

Reddit is even more blunt. In a long, highly-upvoted seller thread on r/feethustle titled “FunwithFeet Review: My Experience As A Seller,” the consensus is harsh.

One seller wrote that they gave it “a fair try for like 3 months” and it “did NOT get better,” adding that they much prefer FeetFinder and make a few hundred dollars a month there.

Another said Fun With Feet is “not worth it,” that the company seems “mostly after the sellers subscription fee,” and that “they have almost no buyers on the platform.”

Several commenters describe switching to FeetFinder and only then starting to make sales, and a few use the word “scam” to describe their own experience of paying and earning nothing.

You should weight this the right way. Anonymous reviews aren't proof, invited five-star reviews aren't fake, and a few loud negatives don't define a platform.

But when the positive reviews cluster around “easy sign-up” and the negatives cluster around “no buyers, no traffic, and trouble getting paid,” that split is the most useful signal you have — and it lines up exactly with the storefront-versus-marketplace problem.

Fun With Feet Pros: What Genuinely Works

A fair review names the real strengths, and Fun With Feet has several:

  • A no-commission earnings model: The platform states sellers keep 100% of sales, with the cost being the subscription rather than a percentage. For a seller who already has buyers, that's genuinely attractive.
  • Mandatory ID verification: Every creator is identity-verified, which raises the floor on authenticity and keeps out some bad actors.
  • Real anonymity: You can sell feet pics without ever showing your face, using a pseudonym and feet-only content. In this niche, that privacy is a core need.
  • A tight, feet-only niche: No general nudity, no unrelated categories competing for attention. Buyers there want exactly what you sell.
  • A genuinely easy setup: The sign-up flow is quick and beginner-friendly — exactly what most positive reviews praise.
  • A UK-registered operator and clear policies: GYCO Online Limited is registered in England and Wales, and publishes terms, a refund policy, a content-complaints process, and DMCA and 2257 statements, committing to resolve content complaints within seven business days.
  • Low upfront cost to test: The subscription is inexpensive, so trying the platform isn't a big financial commitment.

Fun With Feet Cons: The Real Limitations

These are the issues that show up again and again across independent reviews and the platform's own documentation:

  • No organic buyer discovery: The core problem. The platform doesn't surface new profiles algorithmically, so a creator with no outside audience will struggle to generate sales. It's structural, and it makes Fun With Feet a poor starting platform for anyone building from zero.
  • A small buyer base: The platform advertises 8,000-plus buyers — modest in this market. Reviewers consistently describe far fewer buyers than on larger sites, which means less demand even if you do drive traffic.
  • Documented payout problems: Multiple dated Trustpilot reviews describe requesting earned payouts and not receiving them for weeks, with support going silent. This is the most serious concern on the list, because it's about money you've already earned.
  • A glitchy site, especially on mobile: With no dedicated app, everything runs in the browser, and reviewers describe the upload experience as awful on a phone and the site as crashing.
  • A refund policy that excludes the most common complaint: The refund policy states refunds won't be granted if “a user did not receive the sales or earnings they expected” or if “creator earnings are lower than anticipated.” In plain terms: pay the subscription, make nothing, get nothing back.
  • Limited support responsiveness: Several sellers report slow or ignored support, particularly around payouts.
  • Limited security transparency: For a platform that collects government ID and processes payments, there's limited public detail on data protection and security practices — worth weighing before you upload your ID.

Honest framing: None of this makes Fun With Feet an outright bad actor. It makes it a small storefront with small-platform problems — and one policy and payout pattern that new sellers, in particular, shouldn't ignore.

Fun With Feet Refund and Cancellation Policy

Because Fun With Feet sells access to digital services, its refund policy (effective 5 March 2026) is restrictive, and it's worth reading before you pay.

Refunds may be granted for fraudulent or unauthorised transactions, duplicate payments, billing-system errors, or a verified technical fault that prevents access to purchased content.

Refunds are explicitly not granted if you simply change your mind, cancel after a billing cycle has started, are dissatisfied with the service, or — most importantly for sellers — if “a user did not receive the sales or earnings they expected” or “creator earnings are lower than anticipated.”

That last part is crucial: the single most common seller complaint, paying and not earning, is specifically excluded from refunds.

To cancel a Fun With Feet subscription, do it from your account settings before your renewal date so you're not billed for the next period, and keep a written record of the request.

Interestingly, some sellers who struggled to get payout support answered still reported that their subscription cancellation was processed promptly — so the cancellation itself is usually the easy part.

The practical lesson: never treat the subscription as refundable insurance. Treat it as money spent, and only spend it if you already have a way to bring buyers.

Fun With Feet Payment Methods, Withdrawals and Payout Timeline

When a buyer purchases your content, the money is credited to your Fun With Feet balance, and you then request a withdrawal to your bank.

Buyers pay with major cards, including Visa, Mastercard, and Maestro, through the platform's encrypted checkout, so you're never handling a buyer's card details directly.

The weak spot is on the payout side. Bank transfer is the primary withdrawal route, and details on alternatives such as international options aren't clearly published.

That matters if you're outside the platform's core markets: on Reddit, sellers from countries including those in South America describe struggling to fund a subscription without a standard credit card, or to get a payout method approved at all. Check whether your country and bank are supported before you pay.

Just as important, Fun With Feet doesn't publish a clear payout timeline or service-level commitment. Creator reports vary widely, and — as covered earlier — several sellers describe withdrawals sitting unpaid for weeks with no explanation.

Without a published schedule, you can't plan your cash flow with confidence, which is a real drawback for anyone treating this as income rather than pocket money.

In fairness, no platform is perfect on availability: FeetFinder is available in many countries but not every single one, so international sellers should confirm support there too.

The difference is that FeetFinder publishes a weekly payout schedule, which removes most of the uncertainty Fun With Feet sellers describe around getting paid.

Is Fun With Feet Safe? Privacy and Security

On the basics, Fun With Feet is reasonably safe to use. It verifies identities, keeps sellers anonymous behind a display name, processes payments through the platform rather than peer-to-peer, and advertises encrypted, discreet transactions.

That's meaningfully safer than trying to sell through social-media DMs, where scams and chargebacks are rampant.

The weaker areas are transparency and buyer-side friction. For a platform that collects government ID and handles payment data, there's limited public detail on its security and data-protection practices — something privacy-conscious sellers should factor in.

And while buyer anonymity protects buyers, it can leave sellers dealing with lowballers and time-wasters.

Selling feet pictures is legal in most countries, but the content and age-verification rules you face depend on your own location, so check local laws before you start.

For comparison, this is one area where a larger platform tends to do better: FeetFinder verifies both buyers and sellers by ID and age, runs anonymous, PCI-compliant checkout, and publishes clearer trust and safety information — which reduces both fraud and the volume of non-serious buyers you have to filter.

Selling Feet Pics Safely: Legal and Practical Tips

Whichever platform you choose, a few habits protect your income, privacy, and peace of mind. Whether you sell feet photos on a marketplace or a storefront, these apply to Fun With Feet, FeetFinder, OnlyFans, and anywhere else:

  • Watermark your previews: Free preview images are the most likely to be copied and reshared. A discreet watermark deters theft without ruining the preview.
  • Protect your anonymity deliberately: Keep your face, tattoos, unique jewellery, and identifiable backgrounds out of shots if you want to stay private. Use a pseudonym, and never share personal contact details.
  • Keep every payment on-platform: The most common scam is a buyer trying to move you off-site or asking for gift cards or a direct bank transfer, often “as a deposit.” Legitimate buyers pay through the platform. On-platform payment protects you from chargebacks and fraud.
  • Prefer platforms that verify both sides: Two-sided ID and age verification dramatically reduces scammers and time-wasters — one of the clearest safety advantages a marketplace like FeetFinder has over lighter-verification setups.
  • Know your local law: Selling feet content is legal in most places, but rules differ by country and, in the US, increasingly by state, where age-verification requirements for adult platforms are expanding.
  • Treat it as a real business: Income from selling content is taxable in most jurisdictions. Keep records of your earnings and expenses, and speak to a tax professional about your specific situation.

None of this is meant to scare you off; selling feet content is a legitimate way to earn. The sellers who last are the ones who stay anonymous by design, keep their money on secure platforms, and treat the whole thing professionally.

Final Verdict: Should You Join Fun With Feet in 2026?

Fun With Feet is not a bad platform, and it's not a scam. It's a legitimate, UK-registered, feet-only storefront that works genuinely well for one kind of seller: an established creator with their own audience who wants a low-commission place to convert existing fans into buyers.

The platform doesn't bring you buyers, the buyer base is small, the site can be glitchy on mobile, the refund policy specifically excludes the most common complaint, and a number of sellers have documented real trouble getting paid.
